title: Getting started & Navigation
text:
<>
Welcome to WikiHub — the central documentation and team
knowledge hub. To get started, sign in with your registered username or
email address.
Press Ctrl + K (or ⌘ + K on
macOS) anywhere in the application to instantly open Global Search.
Type keywords, space names, or page titles to jump directly to any document.
Search looks for your words inside space names/keys/descriptions and page
titles/content, ignores accents and capitals (giam sat finds
Giám sát) and forgives small typos in titles. You can type a whole
question, such as ip của Tessel Abbott là bao nhiêu? - filler words
are ignored. Rarer words count for more (in tài khoản cloud của nuti
the word nuti decides), a match in the title counts
extra, and a page is only listed if it covers most of what you typed. Common
Vietnamese and English pairs are treated as the same word - tài khoản
finds Account, cài đặt finds install - and
the words found are highlighted in the results, with the passage that has them
shown under the title. If an administrator has set an
Semantic search (see AI assistant), search also finds pages by
meaning, even when they share none of your words. It does not
currently search attachment filenames or attachment content, and only ever shows
results you have permission to see. There are no date, space, or author filters.
Key Interface Regions:
Top Navigation Bar: the search pill (opens the same
Ctrl+K modal), a Help link (book
icon, takes you here), a notification bell (what has
happened to you - see Notifications), the Light/Dark theme toggle, and
your user menu.
Left Sidebar Rail: Home and
Spaces (plus Requests for accounts linked to an
admin mailbox), then your Most visited spaces -
an automatic, server-ranked list based on which spaces you actually open,
not a manually pinned one - and, for admins, an
Administration section.
Sidebar Collapse: click the collapse/expand button, or
drag the sidebar's right edge past its minimum width, to shrink it to
icons-only. Your preference is remembered on this device.
),
},

title: Spaces, Access Rights & Roles
text:
<>
A Space is a dedicated knowledge container for a specific
team, department, or project. Every page in WikiHub belongs to a space.
“Spaces keep team documentation organized and isolated with custom
access rules, member permissions, and unique space keys.”
Space Management Capabilities:
Creating a Space: Users with space-creation rights can
click Create Space in the Spaces directory. Specify a
unique Space Key (e.g., ENG,
PRODUCT), space name, description, and custom emoji or
vector icon.
Space Visibility (set from
Edit space > Access & Permissions):
Open: every signed-in user
gets full read and write access automatically -
View, Add/Edit, Delete,
Delete own and Move - with no need to grant
anyone anything individually. The two permissions that could
reconfigure the space itself, Admin and
Restrictions, are never handed out for free in either
mode - only a space Owner or someone explicitly promoted holds them.
Restricted: nobody has
anything by default - the permission tables below become the sole
source of who can view, edit, delete, or move anything.
Switching between the two is immediate and non-destructive: a
Restricted space's permission tables stay exactly as configured while
the space is Open, so flipping back and forth never means rebuilding
them from scratch.
Space Owner: every space always has at least one Owner
(the creator, by default) - a protected Administrator that cannot be
removed down to zero, so a space can never end up with nobody able to
manage it no matter what happens to the permission tables below. Manage
the list from Edit space > General; only an existing
Owner can add or remove another one. A space can have several Owners at
once, and each one bypasses every page-level restriction the same way a
Admin grant does.
Per-user & per-group permissions: instead of a fixed
list of named roles, WikiHub grants specific capabilities directly to a
user or a group - View, Add/Edit,
Delete, Delete own, Restrictions,
Move, and Admin - from a space's own
Edit space > Access & Permissions tab, or from
Administration > Spaces (see
Space Access & Effective Permissions for the full picture,
including how to check any one person's resolved access). Exporting a
page follows View automatically, with no separate grant to
hand out. While the space is Open, the tables show All
instead of a checkbox for the five permissions Open already grants
everyone - Admin and Restrictions stay live
checkboxes regardless of mode, since those are the only way anyone
becomes an Admin or narrows who can restrict a page.
A direct grant overrides a group's, not adds to it:
groups you belong to combine with each other as usual, but the moment a
user has their own row on a space, that row alone decides
everything for them - group membership stops contributing anything
beyond it. This is how one member of an otherwise broad group (say,
everyone with Add/Edit) can be narrowed to
View only, by giving that person their own smaller row.
Admin is the one exception: a group's
Admin grant always still applies, so a space can never
end up locked with no administrator reachable.
Editing a space: click Edit space
(pencil icon in the space sidebar footer, admins only) for three tabs:
General (name, Space Owner, and an optional per-space
attachment-size limit that overrides the workspace default),
Access & Permissions (General access plus the
tables above), and Space settings & Danger zone
(Archive/Restore the space, or permanently Delete it - permanent
deletion is only available from Administration > Spaces,
not here).
Favouriting: Click the ★ Star icon on a
space's header to add it to your favourites. Favourited spaces show up
under My favorite spaces on the Home page, and under the
Favorite tab of the Spaces directory (
/spaces?tab=starred). The directory's own
Own tab is different - it lists spaces
you own (see Space Owner above), not ones you have starred.
The sidebar's own Most visited list is separate and
automatic - it ranks whichever spaces you actually open most, independent of
what you've starred.

title: Ask AI from search
text:
<>
Quick search can answer a question, not only list pages. Open search (Ctrl+K or
the search bar), type a question such as what is the IP of the DMS SaaS system?
and click Ask AI at the top of the results, or press Ctrl+Enter.
Plain Enter still opens the highlighted result. The row only appears when an
administrator has connected an AI endpoint and the question is at least two characters.
The answer is short and every statement carries a numbered mark such as
1. Click a mark to open the page it came from. A list of several things
(systems with their addresses, accounts, servers) comes back as a table. Under the
answer, Sources lists the pages the marks stand for, one line each - hover a
row to see the part of the page that was read. Also read is folded away
below it and lists pages that were only looked at, never cited, so they cannot be taken
for sources.
Going back: Results or Esc returns to the normal
results (a second Esc closes search). Changing the question leaves the answer,
because it belongs to the question it was written for.
What it reads: only pages you can open. Page and space permissions apply
exactly as in normal search, so a restricted page is never read on your behalf.
Passwords, tokens and keys are replaced with [hidden] before the AI reads
them and again in what it writes - open the source page to see them yourself.
When there is no answer, it says so and offers the pages that may help.
WikiHub never shows an answer it cannot tie to a page: a reply with no valid page mark is
discarded.
Cost: a question uses the same hourly limit as the other AI features.
Asking the same thing again within an hour, while the pages are unchanged, is served from a
saved copy and costs nothing. A question that matches no page never reaches the model.
Administrators see these under Questions answered in the AI usage statistics.
The AI can misread a page. Open the sources before you rely on an answer for something that
matters.
),
},

title: Chat with the AI assistant
text:
<>
When an administrator has connected an AI endpoint, a Chat with AI button (a
sparkle icon) appears in the top bar of every page, next to the notifications. It opens a panel on the right where you
can ask a question and keep asking: a follow-up such as and its address? is
understood from the earlier messages. The reply appears word by word, and
Enter sends (Shift+Enter starts a new line).
Sizing: drag the left edge of the panel to make it wider or narrower
(double-click the edge to reset it), use the expand button for the whole page, or use the
arrow keys on the edge. Clicking outside the panel puts it away; your conversation stays.
Where answers come from: first your wiki, with numbered marks such as
1 that open the page and a Sources list, exactly as in search.
Facts about your own systems, accounts and people come from the wiki only.
The internet: if an administrator turned on web search, the chat may look up
a public, technical question the wiki does not cover. You see
Searching the web for ... with the exact query, and the answer lists the pages
under From the web with marks such as w1, which open in a new tab.
Only that short query leaves WikiHub - never a wiki page - and addresses, e-mails and
internal host names are removed from it first. If the search service finds nothing, or
only pages about something else (the free one behind a gateway sometimes does), WikiHub
tries free sources that need no key - the open web (Bing, DuckDuckGo), Google News
headlines and Wikipedia - and reads the text of the pages it finds, again sending only
that short query.
Follow-ups and numbers: earlier messages count as context, so
I am in Cam Ranh after what is the weather today? is understood.
When a question lacks something it depends on (a city), the assistant asks first. For the
weather it reads real measurements (temperature, humidity, wind, chance of rain) and
names the source; for other questions it also reads the text of the top web pages, not
only their descriptions, so figures on them can be quoted. Pages are only fetched from
public addresses.
General knowledge: when neither the wiki nor the web answers and the
question is general, the AI may answer from its own knowledge. Such an answer is always
marked Not checked against your wiki or any web page; treat it as a hint.
Explain or translate: select a word, phrase or sentence in a question or
an answer and the small AI button appears at the end of it, as on a page. It explains the
words (in Vietnamese by default) or translates them; the globe button switches the
language. Nothing is sent until you choose, and asking again is free.
It knows your account. Ask which spaces can I open?,
what is my role in OPS?, how do I change my password? or
why can't I see a page? and it answers from your own spaces,
roles and permissions and from how WikiHub works, with buttons under the answer that
open the page you need (Spaces, your account, the user guide - and, for
administrators, the matching Administration page). It only ever reads your own
account, and shows administration buttons only to people who may open them.
It can do things for you. Ask create a space called abc and
write a Prometheus guide in it and it shows a short plan - for example
Create space "abc", then Write the page "Prometheus
guide" (the page is drafted by AI) - with Confirm and run and
Cancel. Nothing changes until you confirm, and it runs with your own
permissions: what you could not do by hand it will not do, and a step you are not
allowed to take is listed as not offered. It can create spaces and pages, add someone
to a space with a role, and star a space. Each finished step has an
Open link. If a step fails, the ones after it are not run.
It reads this guide. Questions about how WikiHub works (backups,
permissions, uploads, shortcuts...) are answered from the sections of this Help page.
If the feature belongs to administrators and you are not one, it says so and who to
ask.
It decides where to look. When the internet is allowed, a question
about now or the news (today, yesterday, a date, prices, weather) or one your wiki does
not clearly hold is sent to the web before an answer is written; questions about your
own wiki and your account are answered from them. A reply that came to nothing gets a
second look, and the choice for a question is kept for ten minutes, so asking again goes
the same way.
How much detail. Under the box, choose Brief (just the
key point), Balanced or Detailed (steps, values, examples and
limits). The choice is kept in this browser and applies to the next question; to see an
earlier answer at another level, change it and press Answer again on the
question.
Easier to read. Answers are laid out to be scanned: the answer in a bold
first sentence, steps as a numbered list, a table when several things have several facts
each, code for what to type, italics for a term, a quote for words
taken from a page, coloured notes (Tip, Warning, Important, Note) for what must not be
missed, and a highlighter on the one value that matters. Colour is kept for those; the
rest is plain.
It stays open. The panel stays open when you go to another page - also
through the buttons it shows - and with your conversation in it. It closes only when you
click outside it, press Esc in it or use the X.
Earlier questions. In the box, press ↑ to bring back the
question you asked before, again for the one before that, and ↓ to come
forward - back to what you were typing. The cursor goes to the end, so you can change
it and send it. In a question of several lines the arrows move inside the text.
Your conversation is kept only in this browser, for your account, and is removed
when you sign out or switch account. Use
New chat to clear it. Stop cancels a reply: the question stays,
with what was written and a note that you cancelled it, and Try again asks
it once more. Hover a question and press Answer again to get a
fresh answer; the earlier one stays under the 1 / 2 arrows to go back to. From a search answer, Continue in chat carries it on.
Administrators find the switch under Administration, AI assistant,
Web search: choose the AI gateway's own search (no key), Tavily, Brave
Search or Serper (paste the key) and use Test search, which tries the
service you chose on its own. It is off by default. A paid service is more reliable than
the free one behind a gateway.
The AI can be wrong, and web pages can be wrong too. Open the sources before you rely on an
answer for something that matters.
),
},

title: Finding pages you've visited, edited, or saved
text:
<>
Beyond the workspace-wide activity feed on Home, WikiHub keeps
three personal views of your own history:
These pages exist and work today, but there is no menu item pointing at them
yet - bookmark whichever ones you use.
Recently visited /recent/visited
: pages you've opened on this device, most recent first. Stored in this
browser only, like Save for later below.
Recently worked on /recent/worked-on
: pages you personally created or edited. This one is pulled from the
server, so it is the same list on every device you sign in from.
Saved for later /saved
: everything you've bookmarked with the Save for later
button (see Liking, saving & sharing a page below).
Home itself (the logo, or Home in the
sidebar) shows a different, workspace-wide view: All updates -
every page anyone has edited, grouped by author - alongside your favourite
spaces in the right-hand panel.
),
},

title: Liking, saving & sharing a page
text:
<>
Below a page's title, the page toolbar carries a small set of actions
separate from editing:
Like: click the thumbs-up above the comments, beside the
comment count, to flag a page as useful. The count is visible to everyone and
the icon fills in blue once you have liked it - a lightweight signal for what
actually gets read, not a moderation tool. Click the number beside
the thumb to see who liked the page. Clicking the speech-bubble count next to it
jumps to the comment box, which stays pinned to the bottom of the screen while you
read so you can comment from anywhere on the page.
Save for later: click the star
Save for later button to bookmark a page.
Saved-for-later status lives in this browser, not your account - saving on
your laptop will not show up on your phone, and clearing browser data
clears it too. Everything you've saved is listed at
/saved.
Share: click Share and pick an option.
Copy link puts the page's direct link on your clipboard, ready to
paste into chat or email. Share with people… opens a picker: search by
name or username, pick one or more colleagues, then click Share - each
of them gets a notification saying you shared the page, and the link opens it.
Sharing never grants access: on a restricted space or page, people who can't
open it are listed greyed out with a lock and
No access to this page or space, and can't be picked. Every person you
share with adds one to the share count beside the like and comment counts under the
page; click that count to share again. A space overview only has
Share to copy its link.
TL;DR: click TL;DR in the toolbar for a short AI
summary of the page, written in Markdown (bold key terms, code, lists). The summary is
saved until the page changes, so reopening it is instant; Summarize again
asks for a fresh one. The summary is in the page's own language; the switch at the
top changes it to English or Tiếng Việt (and
Page language goes back). Switching only translates the summary you already
have, which is quick and light on the AI; only Summarize again reads the
page and writes a new one. Web addresses in the summary are links, and the name of a file
attached to the page opens that file - to view it, or to edit it too if you can edit
the page. The i beside the title says the summary can miss
details. It only reads pages you can already open, and each person gets a limited
number of new summaries per hour. Until an administrator connects an endpoint it
explains that the assistant isn't set up yet.
Page access: on a page you can manage, click
Page access to open its General access setting -
Open or Restricted - plus the table underneath it,
which looks different depending on which one is picked:
Open (the default) lists every person and group the
space already grants access to, with their current View/Edit access to
this page pre-checked - nothing to search for or add. Unchecking a box
blocks just that person or group; everyone else is unaffected. Edit is
greyed out for anyone whose space role does not include it, since a
page restriction only ever narrows who edits among people the space
already lets edit - it never grants editing beyond that. Both View and
Edit are greyed out (and pre-checked) for a space Admin, since Admins
bypass every page-level restriction - blocking one here would not
actually do anything, so the box is locked instead of offering a
control with no effect.
Restricted instead starts from an empty allow-list you
build up by searching and adding specific people or groups - anyone
not added cannot see the page at all, regardless of their space role.
View and Edit restrictions flow down to every child page. A child with no
restrictions of its own follows its parent: whoever can view or edit the
parent can do the same on the child, and nobody else can. Opening
Page access on such a child shows General access as
Inherit parent, names the parent, and lists only the
people the parent lets in, read-only - View and Edit both follow the parent.
Pick Restricted (own list) to give this page a list of its own - the
first time, a draft table pre-filled from the parent opens, and nothing applies
until you press Save list. From then on that list decides for the page
(and its children): people on it can view and edit it even if the parent never let
them in, and people only on the parent's list do not get in. Blocks set on
pages above still apply.
Every child page has an Inherit permissions from parent page
switch, on by default. Turn it off and the page copies its parent's
access first - nobody gains or loses anything at that moment - then keeps
its own settings: add people the parent never allowed, or remove some. Its
own children follow it, not the pages above it. Turning the switch back on
(confirmed first) clears the page's own settings and follows the parent
again.
The line at the very bottom of every page answers it: for example
11 users and 1 group can view this page, counted after the
page's own restrictions and everything it inherits. When nothing narrows
an Open space it reads All users and all groups can view this page.
The Space overview shows the same for the space itself.
Neither table's checkboxes can be clicked until you press its own
Edit button - a stray click cannot change anyone's
access. Press Done when you are finished with that table to
lock it again.
Flip General access back and forth as much as you like - whatever
Restricted allow-list or Open blocks you had configured comes right back
each time, instead of being rebuilt from scratch. Reset to default
(with a confirmation first) is the deliberate way to actually clear
whichever mode is currently active: Restricted resets to an empty
allow-list, Open clears every block.
It only lets you search and pick people or groups the space itself has
already granted access to - restricting a page to someone still locked
out at the space door would do nothing but confuse. Anyone else you
search for still shows up, greyed out and marked
Not added to space; add them under the space's own
Access & Permissions first, then come back here. In an
Open space everyone already has access, so every user and
group can be picked straight away. If someone
is later removed from the space entirely, any page-level restriction or
block naming them is cleaned up automatically.
Real-world use cases: a space stays open to the whole team, but the one page
documenting an incident postmortem or a compensation policy gets switched to
Restricted and limited to just the people who need it. Or the
opposite - a page stays Open, but one person should not see it
(a manager reviewing feedback about themselves) - so just their own View is
unchecked instead.
),

title: Comments, replies & likes
text:
<>
Every page has a Comments section below its content (it is hidden
while you edit the page). Anyone who can view the page can comment, reply and
like - you do not need edit access.
Writing and replying:
Type in the box and press Enter (or Comment) to send;
Shift+Enter starts a new line. Plain text works, and so do **bold**,
_italic_, `code` and links.
Choose Reply under a comment to answer it. Replies sit under the
comment they answer, as a tree; a comment with replies shows
View N replies to open them and Hide replies to fold
them again. Deep threads stop indenting after a few levels so they stay readable. A long
comment (a pasted log, say) shows its first few lines with a blue See more
that opens the rest.
Type @ and a name to mention someone: pick them with
the arrow keys and Enter, or click. They get a notification. On a
restricted space or page, people who can't open it are still listed but greyed out
with a lock and No access to this page - they can't be picked until someone
grants them access.
Liking, editing and deleting:
Click Like under a comment to like it (it turns blue); click it again
to take the like back. Once a comment has likes, a blue thumbs-up badge with the count
sits at the end of that row - click it to see who liked it. The comment's author is
notified once.
Hover a comment and open its ⋯ menu (always visible on touch screens)
to Edit your own comment - it then shows edited.
The same menu has Delete for your own comments. Space owners, space administrators
and system administrators can delete anyone's. Deleting a comment also deletes
all of its replies, and WikiHub asks you to confirm first.
Sorting and filtering:
Once a page has more than one comment, a menu at the end of the like / comment row
(it reads Oldest to start with) orders the discussion by
Oldest, Newest or Most liked - likes
count across the whole thread. Each choice says what it shows.
The same menu narrows to Mentions me or My comments,
each with its count. A thread is kept whole when any comment in it matches, and the
matching replies open automatically. Pick an order again to see everything.
You are notified when someone replies to your comment, mentions you, likes your comment,
or comments on a page you created - click it in the notification bell
and WikiHub opens the page, expands the thread if the comment is a reply, scrolls it into
the middle of the screen and highlights it for a moment. This works even if you are
already on that page. Comments are included in backups and restores.
),
},

title: The “⋯” menu: move, view width, export & delete
text:
<>
Click the ⋯ (More page actions) icon next to
Edit for everything that isn't inline editing:
Move page: pick a destination Space and a
Parent page (searchable, or Top-level page) to
relocate a page anywhere - even into a different space. Its child pages
move with it, and the picker won't let you drop a page inside one of
its own descendants.
Page history: opens the revision timeline (see
Revision History, Visual Diff & Export).
Import from file…: convert documents into new child pages
(see Importing documents as new pages in Attachments & Media).
View → Full width /
Normal width: widen the reading column, useful for pages
dense with tables or screenshots.
Export → HTML / PDF /
Word: see Revision History, Visual Diff & Export
for exactly what each format preserves.
Delete page: permanently removes
the page.
Deleting a page moves any of its child pages up one level rather than deleting
them too - their content always stays reachable.
),

title: Pages, Sticky Toolbar & Source Editing
text:
<>
WikiHub features a state-of-the-art document editor designed for fast,
distraction-free writing.
As you scroll down long documents in edit mode, the editor toolbar
remains fixed at the top of your screen. You can format text, insert
elements, or switch modes at any time without scrolling back up.
Editing Modes & Tools:
Rename a page: click Edit, then click the
title itself at the top of the page - it becomes editable right there,
no separate dialog. The page keeps its existing link when you save, so
anything that already points to it keeps working.
Rich-Text Mode: WYSIWYG editing with full inline
formatting tools:
Bold (Ctrl+B)
Italic (Ctrl+I)
Underline (Ctrl+U)
Strikethrough
Inline Code
Link (Ctrl+K)
Markdown & HTML Source Mode: Click
<Source /> in the editor header to toggle into raw
Markdown or HTML code view. Perfect for pasting technical documents,
inspecting markup, or fine-tuning exact HTML elements.
Automatic Local & Server Drafts: Every keystroke
is automatically saved to your browser's local storage and synced with
the server. If you accidentally close your browser, your draft is
restored seamlessly when you return.
),
},

title: Images, Resizing & File Attachments
text:
<>
WikiHub makes media integration seamless for technical documentation.
You can drag images directly from your computer into the editor surface to upload them instantly.
Image Features:
Corner Resize Handles: Click any image in edit mode to
display visual corner handles. Click and drag the handle to resize the
pixel width dynamically.
Floating Image Toolbar: Hover over any image to access
quick positioning controls: Align Left, Center,
Align Right, and Edit Caption.
Captions: Add descriptive captions below images; captions
are formatted with subtle text for clean presentation.
Click to Zoom: On a published page (not while editing),
click any image to open it full-screen. Scroll or double-click to zoom in
and out, drag to pan around once zoomed, and use the toolbar's
+/- buttons or the reset icon for precise control.
Click anywhere outside the image, press Esc, or use the
X button to close it.
File Attachments:
Upload PDF documents, archives (.zip, .tar.gz), code
files, video, or Office documents the same way. Clicking any attachment opens
the same interactive preview modal - see the
Attachments & Media guide for what each file type can do
once it's uploaded, including in-place Office editing, PowerPoint
slideshows, and video Picture-in-Picture.
),
},

title: Tables, Code Blocks & Interactive Components
text:
<>
Present structured information using advanced interactive blocks.
1. Data Tables:
Hover over table cells to reveal action chevrons for inserting/deleting
rows and columns.
Toggle header row formatting to highlight column titles.
Cells support rich inline formatting (links, bold, inline code).
2. Syntax-Highlighted Code Blocks:
Automatic syntax highlighting powered by Prism/HLJS for over 40
languages (Python, TypeScript, Go, Rust, SQL, Bash, Dockerfile, etc.).
Options Bar: Click the top-right options icon on any code
block to open the Code Block Details Modal to set a language,
title, or line numbers.
1-Click Copy: Readers can click the Copy
button to copy raw code to their clipboard instantly.
3. Collapsible Toggles & To-Do Lists:
Toggle Blocks: Collapse lengthy secondary content (such as
changelogs or raw payloads) under an expandable chevron.
Checkable To-Do Lists: Create task checklists. Clicking a
checkbox toggles its completed state and persists when saved.
),
},

title: Revision History, Visual Diff & Export
text:
<>
WikiHub keeps a complete, immutable audit trail of every change saved to a
page.
Restoring an old revision never deletes history! Restoring creates a brand
new revision with the older content, so all intermediate revisions remain
intact forever.
History Features:
Page History Timeline: Click History in the
page action bar to view a chronological list of revisions with author,
timestamp, and change summary.
Visual Diff Comparison: Select any two revisions to compare
changes side-by-side or inline. Additions are highlighted in green,
and deletions are highlighted in red.
Export: Open Export in page actions to
download the page as PDF, HTML, or Word. PDF and HTML are rendered from
the exact page you see on screen, so colors, fonts, code highlighting,
callouts, and tables come out looking identical to the live page - not a
re-formatted approximation of it.
A collapsed toggle section exports fully expanded, since a static file has
no way to click it open. Word is the one format with a real ceiling: its
.docx format has no equivalent of a CSS rounded corner, shadow, or
gradient, so a callout or code block comes out as a square shaded
paragraph - faithful in color and text, not in exact shape. PDF and HTML
have no such limit.
),
},

title: Draft Auto-save & Recovery
text:
<>
Publishing a page (clicking Save) and merely having unsaved
changes are two different things in WikiHub - a dedicated draft system sits
between them so a closed tab or a crashed browser never costs you real work.
Auto-save toggle: while editing, switch on
Auto-save (in the editor toolbar) to save your in-progress edit
to the server every 30 seconds - separately from actually publishing the
page. A local copy is also kept in your browser as a fallback.
Recovering a draft: if you navigate away (or your browser
closes) with an unpublished draft still pending, coming back to that page
shows a Draft not released banner - “This draft was last
saved on {""} and has not been saved to the page.” Click
Open editor to resume exactly where you left off, or
Discard draft to throw it away.
Conflict warning: if someone else published changes to the
page after your draft was created, the banner adds
“The page has changed since this draft was created.” so
you know to check for overlap before resuming.
Discard draft asks “Discard unreleased draft?”
before doing anything - it only ever removes the saved draft and restores the
page to its current, already-published content.
),
},

title: Switching Between Rich Text, Markdown & HTML
text:
<>
Switching a page's edit mode between Rich text and
Markdown source is not just a different view of the same
data - the underlying content format actually changes, so WikiHub confirms it
first.
Markdown cannot represent every rich-text feature - text colors, cell
backgrounds, and merged table cells have no Markdown syntax. To preserve them
anyway, WikiHub embeds their raw HTML directly inside the Markdown source
rather than silently dropping them. Converting back to HTML is always
lossless.
While editing in Markdown source:
Live preview: toggle a rendered preview of your Markdown
alongside the raw source.
Split / Full layout: choose side-by-side source-and-preview,
or a preview-only view for proofreading before you save.
),
},
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// ATTACHMENTS & MEDIA CATEGORY
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

title: Previewing Files Without Leaving the Page
text:
<>
Click any attachment in a page to open the Attachment details
modal - the same modal for every file type, with a preview panel that adapts
to what the file actually is:
Images: zoom and pan.
PDFs: continuous multi-page viewer with zoom out / actual
size / zoom in, a Rotate pages button (90° steps), and an
expand-to-full-size toggle.
Video: full playback controls plus subtitles, audio-track
switching, and Picture-in-Picture - see
Video: Subtitles, Audio Tracks & Picture-in-Picture below.
Word, Excel & PowerPoint: a faithful rendered preview
(with its own zoom controls) and, while you are editing the page, an
Edit button - see Editing Word, Excel & PowerPoint
in Place below.
Code & text files (.py, .ts,
.json, .md, .log, etc.):
syntax-highlighted with line numbers, a Search content… box
with a match counter and Previous/Next-match navigation (
Enter / Shift+Enter to cycle matches), and a
word-wrap toggle.
Everything else (archives, binaries, unrecognized types):
file details and a Download button.
Hover the ⓘ icon next to the “Attachment details”
title for filename, size, MIME type, and upload date - without opening
Download.
Real-world use case: checking the exact contents of a teammate's
config.json, reviewing a signed PDF contract, or eyeballing a
design PNG - all without ever leaving the wiki page it's attached to.
),
},

title: Editing Word, Excel & PowerPoint in Place
text:
<>
WikiHub can embed a full ONLYOFFICE document editor directly
inside the attachment preview modal for .docx,
.xlsx, and .pptx files - the same ribbon, formulas,
formatting, and slide layouts as the desktop apps, running in the browser.
While editing the page (the Edit button only appears in
edit mode, not for someone just reading the page), open the attachment and
click Edit (pencil icon) next to Download.
Changes autosave as you type - there is no manual Save
button, and the toolbar shows Saving changes… or
{""} · Changes save automatically. Every save bumps
the attachment's revision, so it stays accounted for in the page's
activity.
Click Back to preview to return to the read-only render at
any time.
Other Office formats - .doc, .ppt,
.xls, .odp, .ods, and template variants
like .dotx/.potx/.xltx - preview
correctly but must be edited elsewhere and re-uploaded.
The Edit button only appears when an administrator has configured and
connected an ONLYOFFICE Document Server. If it's missing entirely, or
shows “The workspace document editor is not configured,” ask your
administrator.
Real-world use case: fixing a typo in a shared spec .docx or
updating a budget .xlsx without leaving the wiki or e-mailing a
new copy back and forth.
),
},

title: Video: Subtitles, Audio Tracks & Picture-in-Picture
text:
<>
Click a video attachment to open the standard HTML5 player with play/pause,
seek, volume, and fullscreen.
Subtitles: if the video has caption tracks, a
Subtitles button appears in the preview toolbar - pick a
track, or Off.
Audio tracks: for videos with more than one audio track, an
Audio track picker lets you switch between them (only where
the browser itself exposes multiple tracks - not every format supports
this).
Picture-in-Picture: use the PiP icon in the player's
own controls (or right-click → Picture in Picture) to pop the video
into a small floating window that stays on top of every other window and
tab.
Closing the attachment preview while a video is floating in Picture-in-Picture
does not stop it - exactly like closing a browser tab
doesn't stop a PiP video elsewhere on the web. Leaving PiP (its own
“back to tab” or close control) reopens the preview automatically,
resuming right where you left off. Only closing that reopened preview actually
stops playback.
Real-world use case: watching a recorded demo or training clip in the corner
of your screen while you take notes or reply in chat in another tab.
),
},

title: Presenting a PowerPoint Deck: Fullscreen Slideshow
text:
<>
Open any .pptx attachment - it renders as a paginated deck with a
thumbnail rail on the left and the current slide on the right. Use the
on-screen ‹ › arrows, or ←/→, to move
between slides at any time.
Click Present (the small monitor icon in the toolbar) to
start a fullscreen slideshow: the deck fills the entire screen,
letterboxed to the slide's own aspect ratio, with no browser chrome or
thumbnail rail in the way.
Press Esc, or click the ✕ in the top-right corner,
to exit - back to the normal preview, not the whole attachment window.
Real-world use case: presenting a slide deck straight from the wiki page
it's attached to during a meeting, with no extra software and no
re-downloading the file first.
),
},

title: Importing Documents as New Pages
text:
<>
From any page, open the ⋯ menu and choose
Import from file….
Drag and drop, or browse for, up to 20 files at once.
Supported formats: Word (.docx), OpenDocument Text (
.odt), Rich Text (.rtf), EPUB (
.epub), HTML (.html/.htm), Markdown (
.md/.markdown), and PDF (.pdf).
Each file becomes a new child page under the page you
started from (or at the top level of the space, from Home) - headings,
formatting, and images carry over automatically.
The new page is named after the file name, extension
dropped (Runbook-v2.docx becomes a page titled
Runbook-v2) - not after a heading or title inside the
document.
Import runs as a background job with a live per-file progress indicator
(queued / running / complete / failed), each finished file linking straight
to its new page, so you can keep working while a large batch converts.
Review with AI after importing (on by default; the choice is
remembered). Once a page is made, WikiHub reads the original file again, on its own, and
compares it with the page: text that went missing, a heading of another level, a list
or code or quote that became plain paragraphs, a table that fell apart, repeated page
headers and footers, blocks in another order, and how it looks (an indented line in a table cell turned into a quote, unreadable text on a coloured cell, black forced on every run). What is certain is mended at once; if
the AI assistant is set up, it mends the rest, a few blocks at a time and using the
editor's own formats (lists, tables, code blocks, quotes, callouts). A change is
kept only if the page then matches the file better and lost no text. Each file shows
the result in the progress card (Reviewed: 3 fixes, now it matches the original
or how many differences are left, with notes), and the page as it was converted stays in
its history, so you can restore it. Word, HTML and PDF files are reviewed; the other
types are imported as before. A clean file costs no AI call, and a review that fails
never costs the import. While a file is being reviewed its card shows a live log
(Reading the original file again... Compared 439 blocks with 314: 14 differences...
Asking the AI assistant about 12 differences... 3 changes proposed, 2 kept), and the
same log stays under the file as Review log once it is done. Lists keep their
nesting too: Word indents by how far in a paragraph sits, which the converter ignores, so
the review reads those indents again and nests the list as the file does.
Translate with AI turns each page into English or
Tiếng Việt once it has been made (the default keeps the document's own
language). The AI assistant translates the text piece by piece — every paragraph,
list item, table cell and heading — and each piece goes back only if its tags, links,
image sources and code are exactly as they were, so tables, lists, images, colours and
widths of the page do not change; code blocks and inline code are never translated, and
product names and abbreviations are kept. It runs after the review, shows a live
Translation log on the file's card, and the page in its own language stays
in its history. A piece the model got wrong is left in its own language and counted. It
needs the AI assistant to be set up; a document already in the language you chose is not
translated, and a very large one is skipped. Both options sit under AI options in
the import dialog, each with a one-line summary and an i button that
explains it in full on hover; Original language keeps the text as it is.
Translating is many small calls, so it has its own hourly allowance, and the page title
stays the file's name. If a translation says it could not finish, import the file
again.
This is different from Confluence Archive Import under
Administration > Backup: that one restores a whole
exported Confluence space, including permissions and history, and is
admin-only. Import from file… converts individual documents
into fresh pages, and is available to anyone who can edit the space.
Real-world use case: migrating a folder of existing Word or PDF runbooks into
the wiki as a properly organized page tree, in one pass.
),
},

// ACCOUNT CATEGORY
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

title: Profile, Password Security & Active Sessions
text:
<>
Manage your personal account preferences under Account
from the profile menu.
A member's profile opens with a contribution chart: one square per day
over the last year, darker on days with more page edits. Hover a square for its date and
count, and pick another year on the right to look further back.
In the activity feed, a page you edited several times in a row appears as one row,
Updated 6 times. Click it to see every edit with its own
view change link.
1. User Profile Settings:
Click Edit profile to update display name, email, avatar
image, bio, pronouns, company, and social links.
Field validation provides instant feedback on format or requirement errors.
2. Password Security & Rules:
Update your password in Password & authentication.
Password strength meters check length, numbers, symbols, and uppercase
character rules. Click Generate password to create a strong
random password.
3. Active Sessions Management:
In Sessions, view active browsers and sign out all other
sessions if you see activity you do not recognise. You can revoke specific
devices or click Revoke all sessions to invalidate
all remote tokens immediately.
),
},

title: Notifications: the Bell and Pop-ups
text:
<>
The bell in the top bar tells you what has happened
to you. It is there for everyone, not only administrators. A red number on
it counts what you have not read yet.
What you are told about:
Being added to, removed from, or given a different role in a space.
Being given or losing a specific permission on a space, or becoming (or ceasing to be) a space owner.
Being added to or removed from a group.
An administrator resetting your password.
Your workspace role or permissions being changed, or your account being switched back on.
For System Administrators: every new request from the sign-in page.
Something you do yourself does not notify you. Notifications are shown in your own
language and only you can see yours.
Using the bell:
Open it to see the latest, newest first. Each has a coloured icon - green for good
news (you were added or given access), blue for a change, amber for something taken
away or a password reset - and how long ago it happened.
Click one to read it: if it leads somewhere (a space, Requests) you go there, and it
stops counting as unread. Mark all as read clears the lot.
Pop-ups:
A new notification also appears as a pop-up in the bottom-right corner within a few
seconds - you do not need to reload. Every message the app shows (saved, failed, and so
on) uses the same style, coloured for what it says: green for success, blue for
information, amber for a warning, red for an error. Several at once form a compact
stack; hover over it and they line up in a column, none overlapping, so you can read
each in full. Each pop-up has its own ten-second timer, shown by the bar under its
text: hovering a pop-up pauses that one only, and the timer carries on from where it
stopped when you move away. When it runs out, the pop-up slides off to the right. Use the small x to close one sooner.
),
},

title: Reporting Issues
text:
<>
WikiHub is new, so you may hit a problem. Open your account menu (your
name, top right) and choose Report issue. Give it a title, say what
you were doing and what went wrong, and add screenshots if you can: use
Add image, or simply paste a screenshot with Ctrl+V.
Up to five PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP images of 5 MB each. Use Labels to
tag it - bug, question, enhancement and so on - so it is easy
to find later.
Following your report:
My issues (also in the account menu) lists everything you reported,
with its status - Open, In progress or Done - and who took it.
You get a notification when an administrator takes or is given your issue, and when it
is closed - and an email too when it is closed. If the administrator
left a closing note, you can read it under the issue and it is quoted in the email.
Only you and the people who manage issues can see your issue.
For people who manage issues:
Superusers, system administrators and anyone given the
Manage issues permission (Administration > Groups, or a user's
Global access) see Administration > Issues and are told when a new
one arrives.
Whenever someone reports an issue, everyone who can manage issues is told by
notification and by email.
Tick one or more issues in the list (the box at the top ticks the whole page) to
change them together: Mark as opens, reopens or completes them, and
Assign hands them to someone - only a superuser can give an issue to
another person. Anything you are not allowed to change is skipped and counted, not a
reason to stop the rest.
Pick a view on the left - Issues, Assigned to me or
Created by me - switch between Open and
Closed, and narrow by author, assignee, label (tick
several to require all of them, or pick No labels) or order. The search box
looks in titles and descriptions only, and marks in blue what matched.
Open an issue and choose Take it to put your name on it. It then
counts as in progress. Use Add note for notes only managers see. When you press
Mark done, a closing note box appears for what the
reporter should read; confirm to close the issue.
Only the person who took an issue, or a superuser, can mark it
done, reopen it or otherwise change its status. A system
administrator who has not taken it can read it, not close it.
To hand an issue to someone outside WikiHub, press Export Word - in
the issue window, or next to each issue on My issues. The .docx
holds the title, a details table (status, labels, reporter, assignee, dates, page
link), the description, every screenshot embedded in the file, and the notes shared
with the reporter. Internal notes are never included. The document's labels follow
your interface language. To send several at once, tick them in the list and press
Export Word in the selection bar: you get one file with a summary
table first, then a numbered chapter per issue.
),
},

title: Switching the Interface Language
text:
<>
Click the EN/VI badge in the top bar
to open the language menu, then pick English or
Tiếng Việt. The badge always shows the language
currently active.
Every label, button, toast, and validation message across WikiHub comes
from the chosen language - there is no partially-translated screen.
The change applies immediately, with no page reload, so anything you
were mid-edit in the page editor is left exactly as it was.
The choice is remembered per browser (not tied to your account), so
switching computers or signing in elsewhere starts from English again
until you pick Vietnamese there too.
),
},

title: Customising Keyboard Shortcuts
text:
<>
WikiHub's shortcuts are defaults, not fixed rules. Open
Account from the profile menu and choose
Keyboard shortcuts to change any of them.
1. Rebinding a shortcut:
Click the key badge next to the action you want to change - it switches to
Press keys…
Press the combination you want. It is captured and saved the moment you press
it; there is no separate Save button.
Press Esc to back out without changing anything.
2. Several keys for one action:
Click + to give an action a second (or third) combination - handy
when you want both an old habit and a new one to work. Global search ships this
way, answering to both Ctrl+K and Ctrl+
F. Remove one with the ✕ beside it; the last remaining
binding cannot be removed, so an action is never left unreachable by accident.
3. Getting back to normal:
A circular arrow appears beside any action you have changed - click it to
restore just that one. Reset all to defaults at the top
restores every shortcut at once.
4. Where each shortcut applies:
Each action lists the context it works in - anywhere in the app, while editing a
page, or while an attachment preview is open. Two actions in
different contexts may safely share a combination, and the narrower one
wins while it is active. That is exactly how Ctrl+F works
by default: normally it opens global search, but while you have a text file
preview open it searches inside that file instead.
If you assign one combination to two actions in the same context, a
warning appears at the top and both badges turn amber. Whichever action
handles the key first wins, so the other may not fire. Nothing stops you
saving it - the warning is there so a shortcut that has quietly stopped
working is never a mystery.
The hint on the search bar in the top bar follows whatever you have bound, so
it always shows the combination that actually works.
Some combinations are reserved by the browser itself - Ctrl+
W, Ctrl+T, Ctrl+N and
similar. They never reach the page, so WikiHub cannot capture them.
Text formatting keys inside the editor (Ctrl+B for bold
and friends), / for the slash menu, and Esc for closing
overlays are also fixed and do not appear in this list.
Your shortcuts are stored in the browser you set them in, so they do not
follow you to another computer or survive clearing site data.
),
},
