// ADMINISTRATION CATEGORY
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

title: Theme & Branding Customization
text:
<>
Administrators can fully customize WikiHub's visual identity under
Administration > Settings > Theme & Branding.
The Page Typography & Font Family list keeps similar typefaces
together. Filter it by type - All, Sans-Serif,
Geometric Sans or Serif - and use Show more to see
every font in the group (Show less folds it back to three rows).
Theme modifications stay in draft mode until you explicitly click
Save settings! Click Preview Theme to open an
interactive sandbox modal where you can test colors, search, navigation tabs,
buttons, and Light/Dark mode.
Setting |
Description & Options |
Brand Color Presets |
Choose from 8 curated palettes: Blue, Emerald,
Indigo, Violet, Rose,
Amber, Teal, Slate.
|
Custom Hex Picker |
Enter any custom primary hex color code (e.g., #216fc0).
Generates a full 10-shade HSL palette automatically.
|
Logo Mark Presets |
Select from 9 built-in vector icons: Hub, Book,
Layers, Compass, Sparkles,
Feather, Graduation, CPU,
Shield.
|
Custom Logo Upload |
Upload your organization's custom PNG or SVG image (under 2MB).
Automatically scales and renders across header and favicon.
|
Dynamic Tab Favicon |
HTML5 Canvas converts preset SVGs or uploaded logos into rasterized
64x64 PNG data URLs, updating the browser tab strip instantly.
|
Zero-Flicker SSR |
CSS theme variables are preloaded in <head> on frame 0,
preventing white/blue flash during page refreshes.
|
Font Picker |
Clicking a font in the list opens a Font Specimen
modal - an interactive type tester with a free-text sample input, four
preset sample sentences, five size presets (14–36px), a full
document-hierarchy mockup, and a glyph/character-set matrix - before
you commit with Apply This Font.
|
The Preview Theme sandbox has its own
Light Preview / Dark Preview toggle, so you
can check a brand color against a mock document in both modes before a single
real user sees it.
),
},

title: Statistics
text:
<>
Administrators open Administration > Statistics to see how
the workspace is being used. Pick 7, 30 or 90 days at the top
right; every number and chart on the page follows that range.
Overview
Headline cards: users, people active in the range, new users, pages, spaces,
edits and page views, each with a derived figure underneath (new users in the
range, share of people who were active, average per day, pages per space).
Daily charts of page views, edits and new users, each with its total, the
change from the first half of the range to the second, the daily average and
the busiest day. Hover a chart, or focus it and use the ← and
→ keys, to read each day.
Recent activity: the latest entries from the audit log.
AI usage
Tokens spent by the AI assistant, as reported by the AI gateway: total, prompt
and completion tokens, requests, a daily chart, and a breakdown
by person and by feature (page summaries,
creating a page, the writing assistant, labels and related pages, explaining or
translating a selection).
Pages and Spaces
Ranked tables of the most viewed, starred and
(for pages) saved items. Use Rank by to switch.
Views follow the selected range; stars and saves are all-time totals. A page
counts as starred when people like it, and as saved when people pin it.
Page views and AI tokens are counted from the day this feature was switched on;
earlier activity was never recorded, so a new range can show zeros at first.
Token counts also depend on the AI gateway reporting its usage. Only system
administrators can open this page.
),
},

title: Server monitor
text:
<>
System administrators open Administration > Server to see the
machine WikiHub runs on and WikiHub's own Docker containers. Other services on the
same host are never listed, and their logs cannot be opened - the server refuses the
request, not just the page. The page refreshes every five seconds while it is open
(and not while the tab is hidden).
Server cards: CPU load against the number of cores (with the 5
and 15 minute averages), memory (with swap and what is still available), the disk
holding WikiHub and how much is free, and how long the server has been up with
how many containers are running. Every bar shows its percentage at the right end;
the ones that measure use turn amber at 70% and red at 90%.
Containers: name, short id and image, status (Healthy,
Unhealthy, Running or the state it stopped in, plus how
often Docker restarted it), uptime, CPU and memory. CPU is a share of one core, so
100% is one full core and a busy container on a 12-core server can show more.
Click a column header to sort by it (a number column starts with the biggest;
click again to reverse).
The Logs button opens the last 100 to 1,000 lines of a container.
Filter them, colour shows errors and warnings, Follow refreshes every few
seconds, and the copy button copies what is shown. Passwords, keys, tokens and
credentials in URLs are hidden before the lines leave the server - a best effort,
so still treat logs with care.
This page is read-only: it cannot stop, start or change anything. It is served by
the small ollama-controller service, the only part of WikiHub with access
to Docker, so that service has to be running (./scripts/run.sh --dev).
A container that keeps restarting, or one using far more CPU or memory than expected,
is the first thing to look for when WikiHub feels slow.
),
},

title: Instance Settings & Object Storage Explorer
text:
<>
Administrators configure global workspace behavior under
Administration > Settings, and everything about the S3
bucket - browsing it and setting its limits - under
Administration > Storage.
1. Global Instance Settings:
Site Name: Custom site title displayed in browser tab and top bar.
Session Lifetime (Hours): Configure JWT session expiration (e.g. 24h, 72h, 168h).
Sidebar Access Matrix: Select which navigation sections are visible per user role (member, admin).
2. Storage: Browse files & Quotas:
Administration > Storage splits into two sections, picked from
its own left-hand list:
Browse files: a clean S3 bucket tree browser. Filter objects by
search query, file type, space, or page ID; generate secure pre-signed download
URLs; preview images, video and audio files, code/text files (syntax-coloured by
the file's extension), and Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF documents (opened
read-only through the same document viewer pages use to edit attachments - see
it, download it, nothing is ever saved back from here, and each preview scrolls
in one place rather than in both the dialog and the content underneath it); and
delete orphan objects, which also clears the matching database attachment and
archive hash records automatically.
Quotas: Max single attachment size,
Max backup import size, and
Allowed attachment extensions (a whitelist, e.g.
png, pdf, zip, docx, *) - each shown as
(inherited from environment) until you actually override it here.
),
},

title: Permissions & Roles Reference
text:
<>
Three independent layers decide what any one person can do:
Account role (Member or Administrator),
Global permissions (workspace-wide abilities like
creating spaces or managing users), and Space permissions
(what someone can do inside one specific space). The sections below spell
out each layer; Managing Users & Groups and
Space Access & Effective Permissions (further down) cover the
screens that actually set them.
1. Account roles:
Role |
What it means |
Member |
The default role. What a Member can actually do beyond viewing/editing
the spaces they have access to comes entirely from the Global and Space
permissions below - a Member can hold any of the four global
permissions, or be a Space Owner/Admin, the same as anyone else.
|
Administrator |
Unconditionally holds all four global permissions - Create
spaces, Manage users, Manage groups,
System administrator - regardless of group membership or
any override. An ordinary Administrator cannot Edit, Delete, Demote, or
reset the password of another Administrator account, or change anyone's
Role or Global access overrides for themselves - see
peer-admin protection below.
|
Protected bootstrap admin |
The one account WikiHub is initially set up with (or one explicitly
marked protected). It is always an Administrator, can never be edited,
deactivated, or deleted by anyone else, and is the only
account that can Edit, Delete, Demote, or reset the password of another
Administrator.
|
2. The four Global permissions:
Permission |
What it unlocks |
Create spaces |
Allows creating new documentation spaces from the regular
Spaces directory. It does not open
Administration > Spaces, which stays
System administrator-only.
|
Manage users |
Unlocks Administration > Users: create, edit, reset
the password of, and deactivate Member accounts, and manage
their group memberships. It never promotes/demotes anyone, touches an
existing Administrator account, or opens the Global access
tab - those always require actually being a
System administrator.
|
Manage groups |
Unlocks Administration > Groups: create, update,
assign members to, and manage user groups.
|
System administrator |
Full administrative control - every other Administration section
(Users, Groups, Spaces, Statistics, Settings, Backup, Storage), plus every
per-space Admin permission on every space regardless of
that space's own Owner/Access settings. Equivalent to the
Administrator role for every purpose that matters.
|
Each of the four checks, in order: is the Role already
Administrator? If so, granted outright. Otherwise, does a
per-user Global access override force it
enabled or disabled? An override always wins.
Otherwise, does any group this person belongs to grant it? If none of the
above, it is not granted. See Managing Users & Groups below
for where each of these is actually set.
3. The seven per-Space permissions:
Permission |
What it grants |
View |
See this space and open its pages. Exporting pages
follows View automatically - it is not a separate grant. |
Add/Edit |
Create new pages and edit any existing page in this space. |
Delete |
Delete any page in this space, including ones created by others. |
Delete own |
Delete only pages this person or group created themselves. |
Restrictions |
Restrict individual pages to specific people or groups. |
Move |
Move or reorder pages within this space's hierarchy. |
Admin |
Full control of this space's settings and permissions -
implies every other permission in this table. |
4. Space Owner, Open vs Restricted, and effective access:
Space Owner is a separate, protected tier above the table
above - a space always keeps at least one, and only an Owner (not merely
someone with the Admin permission) can flip a space between
Open and Restricted, or change who the Owners are.
Open spaces grant every signed-in user
View, Add/Edit, Delete,
Delete own, and Move automatically - only
Admin and Restrictions still need an explicit grant.
Restricted spaces grant nothing automatically -
every permission for every person or group comes from the tables in that
space's Access panel.
For a given person and space, the resolution order is: Owner (everything,
always) → a direct per-user grant if one exists (which overrides every
group they belong to for that space, Admin aside) → otherwise
every group they belong to, combined → otherwise whatever Open
hands out automatically. The Effective permissions picker
in a space's Access panel resolves all of this for you instead of
cross-referencing it by hand - see Space Access & Effective
Permissions below.
An ordinary Administrator can fully manage every Member account
- including promoting one to Administrator - but cannot Edit, Delete,
Demote, or reset the password of another Administrator
account. Only the protected bootstrap admin account can touch another
Administrator. This keeps any one administrator from locking out, demoting,
or deleting every other administrator.
),
},

title: Managing Users & Groups
text:
<>
WikiHub does not send invitation e-mails on its own. An administrator creates every
account directly under Administration > Users > Create
user and shares the temporary password with that person out of band
(chat, in person, etc.) - unless the administrator has a working mailbox (see
Administrator Mail & Requests), in which case WikiHub
e-mails the sign-in details automatically, no extra step needed
(the Create user form says so when it is about to happen; the same
applies when setting a new password for an existing account,
promoting someone to Administrator in Edit user, and adding or
removing someone in a space Access tab). A request sent from the
sign-in page works the same way: an administrator with a mailbox
can create the account from their Requests page and have WikiHub
e-mail the username and password to the person.
1. People directory:
The directory shows summary tiles (Total / Administrators / Members /
Active / Disabled), with search and Status/Role filters.
The Last sign-in column shows when each person last signed
in, with a presence marker: Online (active in the last 5
minutes), Offline, or Never signed in. Click the
column header to sort by last sign-in (newest first, click again for oldest
first); accounts that never signed in always stay at the bottom.
Create user: first/last name, username (checked for
availability as you type), e-mail, a password with a live strength
checklist (8+ characters, upper & lower case, a number or symbol), and a
role of Member or Administrator.
Each row has an Edit button opening one dialog for
everything about that account, across three tabs:
General (Role Member/Administrator,
Status Active/Disabled as a switch, an optional new password
with a live requirements checklist - leave both password fields blank to
keep the current one), Groups (below), and
Global access (its Workspace Global Access
overrides - see below). A separate, icon-only Delete button
removes the account entirely. Your own account and the protected bootstrap
admin account never show these controls, so you can never lock yourself out.
The dialog fetches this account's current data fresh each time it
opens, rather than reusing the directory row - reopening right after saving
an override always shows what was actually saved, not what the row still
happened to be showing.
The Groups tab lists every group this account belongs to,
each with a one-click Leave button - and the same
Select / select-all pattern as the directory itself, for
leaving several groups at once. Leaving takes effect immediately, it is not
part of the dialog's own Save.
An ordinary Administrator cannot Edit or Delete another
Administrator account, or reset its password - only the
protected bootstrap admin can. This keeps one administrator from
demoting, deactivating or locking out another; an ordinary
Administrator can still fully manage every Member account,
including promoting one to Administrator.
Holding Manage users without being a
System administrator yourself (whether the account's
Role already is one, or a group/override grants
System administrator) is deliberately narrower: it creates,
edits, resets the password of and deactivates Member
accounts, and manages their group memberships, but the
Role field and the entire Global access
tab are disabled - it can never promote or demote anyone, grant a Global
Access override (an override can hand out
System administrator just as surely as Role can), or touch
an existing Administrator account at all. The only way to
gain any of that is to actually become a
System administrator.
Select (next to the search box) turns on a checkbox per
row and a Delete selected bar for removing several
accounts at once. A protected, your-own-account, or (unless you are
the protected bootstrap admin) another Administrator's
row has its checkbox disabled outright rather than left to fail
partway through a batch.
2. Workspace Global Access overrides:
A Currently granted summary sits above the four
permission rows, listing exactly what this account has right now (or
All permissions (Administrator role) when its Role already
covers everything) - the one place to check before deciding what, if
anything, needs changing below. It, and each row's own
Active/Disabled badge, update the instant you
change Role or an override dropdown - no need to Save and reopen the
dialog just to see whether a choice actually took effect.
The four global permissions (Create spaces,
Manage users, Manage groups,
System administrator) normally come from a user's groups.
The Edit dialog lets you set one of three states per permission, per
person: Inherit from groups (the default), Force
enabled, or Force disabled - the override always wins
over whatever that person's groups say for that one permission.
This has no effect on an account whose Role is already
Administrator: that role unconditionally grants every
permission, the same way it always has.
Manage users unlocks Administration > Users
and Manage groups unlocks Administration >
Groups for that account, whether the permission came from a
group or an override here - each opens only its own matching section,
not the rest of Administration. Create spaces only unlocks
the Create space button on the regular Spaces directory
(see “Creating a Space” above); it does not open
Administration > Spaces, which stays a
System administrator-only oversight view (archive or
permanently delete any space) — same as Settings, Backup and Storage.
3. Administrators tab:
Lists every account that currently holds System administrator
access however it got there - the Role switch, a group's
global permission, or a per-user override - with a
Granted via column saying which. The Role filter on the
People directory only ever shows the first of these three.
Under Granted via, a Role or override grant also names
who did it - the account that flipped the switch or added
the override, read off the audit log. A group grant instead names
which group: group membership and a group's own
permission grants aren't tracked per member, so there is no individual
person to point to there. Either can read as unattributed for an account
that has held its access since before this tracking existed.
Demote to Member undoes whichever of those it was: it
flips Role back to Member for a direct Administrator, or adds
a force-disabled override for one granted through a group or an existing
override. Disabled for the protected admin, your own account, or the last
remaining administrator on the list - and, for a direct Administrator
(Granted via: Administrator role), disabled for anyone except
the protected bootstrap admin, same as Edit/Delete in the People directory.
4. Permission overrides tab:
Lists every account that has at least one Global access
override set - Create spaces, Manage users,
Manage groups, or System administrator, force
Enabled or Disabled for that one account
specifically. Before this tab existed, the only way to find out who had a
customized permission was opening every single account's Edit dialog
and checking its Global access tab one at a time - this tab exists
precisely so that is never necessary.
Each row's Overrides column names exactly which
permissions are overridden and to what value - an account inheriting
everything normally from its Role or groups never shows up here at all.
The same Edit/Delete actions as the People
directory are right there in the row, so acting on what you see - fixing or
removing an override - never means switching back to a different tab first.
5. Groups:
Groups bundle users for reusable space-permission grants - assign a group
once in a space's Access panel instead of adding every
member individually.
Each group can also carry global permissions: Create
spaces, Manage users, Manage groups, System admin.
Group directory and Global access are two
separate tabs above the table, the same split as Administration > Users.
Group directory lists every group; Global access narrows that down to only
the (usually few) groups that actually grant one of the four global
permissions above - the ones worth double-checking before adding someone to
them, out of what is otherwise a much longer list of groups that exist
purely for Space/Page access.
The default system groups (administrators, users,
confluence-administrators, confluence-users)
cannot be deleted, only edited.
A group still granting access to any Space or with a restriction on any
Page cannot be deleted - "Remove this group's permission
assignments before deleting it" means exactly that, and both
have to be cleared first (its global permissions, under Edit > Global
access, don't count - only Space/Page grants do).
The Directory table's Access grants column names how
many Spaces and Pages a group is granted access to - Not used
means it can be deleted outright. Clicking the count opens a quick-view
listing every one of them by name, each linking straight to that Space or
Page, with its own Remove button right there to clear the
grant on the spot - no need to hunt through every Space's Access panel
first. The same list, with the same Remove buttons, is also its own tab
(Access grants) inside the full Edit Group dialog, right
next to Members.
The same Select / bulk-delete control as the People
directory is available next to the group search box; a default system group
stays excluded even when selected.
),
},

title: Space Access & Effective Permissions
text:
<>
Administration > Spaces lists every space with Total /
Active / Archived tiles. Permanent space deletion is only available here (an
individual space's own settings only offer Archive). Open a space's
Access panel to manage exactly who can do what:
Two tabs above the table, the same split as Administration > Users and
Groups: Space directory lists every active space,
Archived spaces lists only the ones hidden from normal
navigation - restore one from its own Edit space > Space settings
& Danger zone, or delete it permanently right from either tab.
General access: Open gives every signed-in
user full read/write access automatically (everything except
Admin/Restrictions) - a warning banner says so
right above the tables. Restricted withdraws that, so only
people explicitly granted access below can do anything.
Space Owner (set from the space's own
Edit space > General tab, not here): a protected
Administrator a space always keeps at least one of, so it can never end
up unmanageable regardless of what happens to the tables below.
A Groups permission table and an
Individual users permission table, each with checkboxes for
View, Add/Edit, Delete,
Delete own, Restrictions, Move, and
Admin. View grants reading only - editing needs
Add/Edit too, and relocating a page needs
Move as well. Exporting follows View
automatically and isn't a separate checkbox. While the space is
Open, the first five columns show All instead -
Open already grants them to everyone, so a checkbox there would not
actually change anything; Restrictions/Admin
stay live regardless of mode. Changes are explicit - Edit, then Save or
Cancel - with an unsaved-changes guard if you navigate away mid-edit.
Effective permissions: pick any user and see their fully
resolved permission set for that space - Open access, any direct grant
(which overrides every group they belong to once they have one, Admin
aside), or otherwise every group they belong to combined - instead of
manually cross-referencing three sources by hand.
Real-world use case: before turning a space Restricted, use
Effective permissions to confirm the one contractor account
that still needs read access actually keeps it.
),
},

title: Switch Account (Impersonation)
text:
<>
Superusers who are not already impersonating someone see a
Switch account control (people icon) in the account menu,
listing other active accounts. Picking one signs you in as them with no
password exchange - useful for confirming “why can't this person
see that page” without asking them to screen-share.
While impersonating, a permanent banner is pinned to the bottom of every
screen: “Viewing WikiHub as {""}. Your actions
are recorded against {""}.” The account menu also shows
Signed in as {""}. Click
Return to my account (in the banner or the menu) to end the
session.
The protected bootstrap admin account and your own account are excluded from
the switch list.
),
},

title: Backup, Confluence Import & DC Export
text:
<>
Administration > Backup has two sections:
Export / Backup and Import / Restore.
1. Two export formats - not interchangeable:
Export WikiHub Backup: a native, restorable
.zip of spaces, pages, revisions, attachments, users, and
groups - scoped to All spaces or a picked subset via
Select spaces to export. It also carries every reported
issue - its labels, status, assignee, notes and screenshots - and
restoring puts them back with the same dates; an issue that already exists is
skipped, never duplicated. Issues belong to the whole workspace, so a backup scoped
to some spaces leaves them out.
Access and discussion come back exactly as they were: space visibility, owners and
every per-user / per-group permission; groups with all their owners, members and
global permissions, and each person's own global-permission overrides; each
page's Open/Restricted setting, whether it inherits from its parent, its
allow-list and its blocks; and every comment and reply with its likes, plus page
likes. Rows that already exist on the target are skipped, never overwritten.
Export Confluence Backup: an XML archive for Atlassian
Confluence Data Center's own restore tooling, targeting
Data Center 8.x or 9.x. This one is a
one-way hand-off - it cannot be used to restore WikiHub itself.
Incoming: this export is switched off for now (the card reads
“Coming soon”) while it is finished.
The WikiHub backup's Include password hashes checkbox is
off by default and explicitly warned as enabling offline password cracking if
the archive leaks - only enable it for an actual migration, and store the file
securely.
2. Restoring / importing:
Both a WikiHub backup restore and a Confluence Archive
Import upload as resumable, chunked, multi-gigabyte transfers with
Pause upload / Resume upload controls -
safe to start, pause, and pick back up later without re-sending what already
made it through.
Confluence import scans the archive for spaces, flags key conflicts, lets
you pick which spaces to bring in, and runs as a background job with live
log output.
A large Confluence archive can take hours to upload. The page keeps your
browser session renewed automatically for as long as that tab stays open -
you do not need to stay logged in manually, and other tabs keep working
normally throughout.
Restoring into an instance that already has spaces triggers a
Replace existing spaces? conflict step for anything that
would collide.
Both upload paths reject a file above a configured size limit (shown on
each card, 1024 MB by default) before uploading starts. A system
administrator can raise it under
Administration > Object storage > Quotas > “Max
Confluence / Backup Archive (MB)”.
A client-side check catches an obviously wrong upload immediately - e.g.
picking a Confluence export under WikiHub restore surfaces
“This is a Confluence export, not a WikiHub backup. Upload it under
‘Import Confluence Backup’ instead.”
before anything even starts uploading. Separately, resuming an interrupted
upload with a different file than the one partially uploaded shows a
“That is a different file” dialog, comparing what
was being uploaded against what you just chose (name, size, how much is
already stored) and asking you to either
Discard and upload this or Choose the original.
3. Automatic backups (scheduled):
The Automatic backups panel, above
Export / Backup, runs a recurring
Export WikiHub Backup on a schedule with no one needing to
click anything.
It writes each backup to a directory mounted into the server itself
(WIKIHUB_AUTOMATED_BACKUP_HOST_DIRECTORY in the deployment's
environment) rather than object storage - a separate copy on separate
infrastructure, so a problem with the primary storage does not also take
out its own backups. Enabled stays greyed out, and
Run now stays disabled, until an operator has actually
mounted that directory.
Subfolder (optional) scopes backups to a folder under that
mounted volume, e.g. team-a writes into <mounted
volume>/team-a instead of the volume's root - useful for keeping
more than one schedule's output apart. The folder must already exist on
the host: Save schedule checks it against the real
filesystem and refuses a path that is missing or that would resolve outside
the mounted volume, with the reason shown right under the field.
Configure Every N hours/days, a Start time
and Timezone (an IANA zone name, e.g.
Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh), and how many completed backups to
Keep - older ones past that count are deleted automatically
as newer ones land. Click Save schedule to apply; the panel
then shows the computed Last run and
Next run times.
Run now queues one immediately without waiting for the
schedule or disturbing it. The list below shows recent scheduled backups
with Download and Delete for each.
Unlike a manual Export WikiHub Backup, a scheduled backup
always includes password hashes - there is no toggle for it, since nobody is
present to opt in each time. Restrict access to the mounted directory the
same way you would any other credential store.
4. Import history and logs:
Under Import / Restore, the Import history
card lists every Confluence import and WikiHub restore - the current one and
all earlier runs - with its status, how long it took, and how many warnings
and errors it logged.
The table is paged (10, 20 or 50 rows per page). Click a column heading
to sort by it, click again to reverse the order, and use the status
filter to show only Failed, Running and
so on.
Click View details on a run to read its full log, oldest line first. Filter to
Warnings or Errors, Copy the
lines, or use Download .txt to save the whole log.
Logs are stored on the server, so a long import that ran while your browser
was closed or asleep can still be explained afterwards. Files that a Confluence
export lists but does not actually contain are counted in a summary line, with
only the first 100 named individually.
),
},

title: AI assistant
text:
<>
For everyone: every page has a TL;DR button in its
toolbar, next to Save for later. Click it for a short summary written in Markdown, in the
page's own language. The switch at the top changes it to English or
Tiếng Việt: that translates the summary already written instead of reading
the page again, so it is quick and cheap. Web addresses in it are links, and a file's
name opens that file on top of the summary. The summary is saved until the page changes, so
reopening it is instant; Summarize again reads the page again and writes a
fresh one. It only reads pages you can already open, and each person gets a limited
number of AI requests per hour (60 unless an administrator sets another limit).
AI in the editor: while you edit a page, put the caret on an empty line
and the hint Press Ctrl+Space for AI or '/' for commands appears. Press
Ctrl + Space to open the AI box, describe what you want - a
checklist, a table of options, an introduction - and press Enter. The AI
writes it, taking the text around the caret into account, and shows it formatted before
anything is added. Then Insert below puts it into the page (replacing the
empty line), or Edit lets you ask for changes - for example
shorter or add a table - as many times as you like. Every version is
kept: the arrows at the top of the box step back and forward between them, and
Insert below uses the one on screen. If AI is not connected yet, the shortcut
shows a small notice that disappears as soon as you carry on typing.
Improve text you already wrote: select text inside one paragraph and a
small AI button appears at the end of the selection (or press
Ctrl + Space). Describe the change - make it more formal,
translate to English - or pick a one-click action: Fix grammar
(spelling, punctuation and grammar, keeping your wording), Consistent terms
(uses the same terms as the related pages already in the wiki, and the same word for the
same thing within your text) or Continue writing (finishes the sentence;
/ → Continue writing with AI does the same at the caret). The
answer is only a suggestion: nothing changes until you click Replace (or
Insert), and it is not applied if the text changed in the meantime.
Edit asks for another version. Only people who can edit the space can use
it, and a plain-text suggestion replaces the selected words, so formatting inside the
selection (bold, links) is not kept - select a smaller part to protect it.
Administrators can set the house style, such as a tone or a glossary, in
Skill management → Writing assistant.
Explain or translate a selection: select a word, phrase or sentence in
a page you are reading and a small AI button appears at the end of the
selection. Click it and the words are explained straight away, in Vietnamese by
default, using the page title and the surrounding text to pick the right
meaning. Use Translate instead to translate the words, and the globe menu
on the card to switch the language between English and
Tiếng Việt - changing it redoes the current action. Answers are remembered
so asking again is instant, and up to 2,000 characters can be selected at a time.
Press Escape or the close button to dismiss the card.
Create a page with AI: in Create page, click
Write with AI (or, after typing a few words in Write,
Draft it with AI to use them as the description), describe the page in a
sentence or two and click Generate. The AI first searches the wiki for
related pages you can read - they are listed on the right - and may ask a few
multiple-choice questions, one at a time: pick an option (hover its i button
for the detail), tick several where allowed or write your own answer, or choose
Skip questions. Your answers are added to the description so you can see
and edit what the draft is built from. WikiHub then drafts the whole page in its own
format - headings, lists, checklists, tables and code blocks - fills in the title if it
is empty and shows a preview you can enlarge. A notice at the very top says the page was
written by AI, so readers know to check it. Nothing is saved until you click
Create page; use Regenerate for another try or
Discard to start over, and edit the page freely afterwards. Only people who
may create pages in the space can use it. Until AI is connected, the tab explains what
is missing instead.
Connect it (System Administrators): open
Administration → AI assistant. The page is a table of saved
connections - any number can be saved, but only one is active at a time.
Add OpenAI Compatible opens a form: a Name, the
Endpoint address of any OpenAI-compatible service including the version
path (for example https://host/v1) and its API key. When you
click out of the address or key field WikiHub checks the connection and lists the
models the service offers - or click Fetch models. Pick the model to use
from the list - the model is always chosen from what the service offers, and
Save stays off until the connection checks out and a model is picked.
Tick Make this the active connection to switch it on straight away.
Semantic search (its own section next to Key management) finds pages by
meaning, not only by words. It is one setting for the whole wiki, separate
from the chat providers, so switching the active provider never rebuilds the index. Choose
where page text is turned into vectors: Active AI provider (if it offers an
embedding model), Another endpoint (an OpenAI-compatible address and key used only
for embeddings, for providers that offer none) or Self-hosted (Ollama). Only
models that can create embeddings are listed, and Save checks that the source
really embeds with the model you pick. WikiHub then indexes every page in the background, a
few at a time, keeps the index current as pages change, and shows progress in the section.
Changing the model rebuilds the index. Leave the model on Off to keep plain
keyword search. Results always respect the permissions of whoever searches.
Self-hosted Ollama runs the embedding model on this server when your provider
has none. Open Semantic search, choose Self-hosted (Ollama), pick a
model (bge-m3 is multilingual and a good fit for Vietnamese) and click
Enable and download. A card shows each step - download Ollama (about 4 GB), start
it, wait until it answers, download the model - with a progress bar; you can leave the page and
it continues. Nothing is installed or running until you enable it, and
Disable stops and removes it so it frees all its memory (about 1-2 GB while
indexing, 0.8 GB idle; capped at WIKIHUB_OLLAMA_MEMORY_LIMIT, 3 GB by default).
The model list is one dropdown: each model is tagged downloaded or not
downloaded, and the i beside it says what the model is good at and when to
pick it - choosing one that is not downloaded turns Save into Download & use.
Cancel stops a download and the card says it was cancelled until you dismiss
the note. Downloaded models stay on disk until you choose Delete downloaded models. This
needs WikiHub's small ollama-controller service, which is the only part with access
to Docker: it can start and stop this one container and nothing else.
In the table, the key is always masked (for example sk-adc2****297a). It
is stored encrypted, never shown again and not included in backups. Edit
changes a connection - leave the key blank to keep it. The Status column
shows Working or Failing from the last check; WikiHub checks
a connection when it is saved or its address or key changes, then re-checks all of
them every five minutes (Not checked only until the first check). Click a column header to sort
(click again to reverse, a third time to go back to the saved order), type in the
boxes under the headers to filter by name, endpoint or model, and use the status
list to show only active, working, failing or not-checked connections. The table
shows ten connections per page.
If semantic indexing misbehaves, read the worker log:
docker compose logs worker | grep search_index. Each minute that
indexed something ends with a search_index_pass line - pages and
chunks done, embed_seconds (time waiting on the AI service),
backlog_remaining and stopped (why it ended). A problem is
a warning: search_index_paused with the service's HTTP
status and reply, ai_embedding_failed for each failed
request, ai_embedding_slow past 10 seconds, and
search_slow (in the backend log) for a search over a second. Page text,
keys and what people searched for are never logged. Set
WIKIHUB_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG to also see every page and request.
The power button makes a connection Active; doing so switches the
previous one off. Switch the active one off and the AI actions are off for everyone.
Check now tests a saved connection and records whether it is
Working or Failing; Remove deletes it
after you confirm.
Labels and related pages: open a page's Page labels
(the tag button under its title) and click Suggest labels and related pages.
The AI reads the page and proposes a few labels - preferring ones you already use on
other pages, which are marked - and lists existing pages that cover the same ground.
Click a label to add it; click a related page to open it in a new tab. After you save an
edit, a small notice offers the same. Labels stay private to your account, the AI only
sees pages you can already read, and the answer is remembered until the page changes, so
opening it again is free.
Skills: open Skill management for one card per AI
skill - Page summary (TL;DR), Create page with AI,
Explain a selection, Translate a selection,
Writing assistant and Labels and related pages. A card
shows only the name and a short description plus whether the skill uses the
Default wording or a Custom one; click it to read the
instructions in full, then Edit to change them, starting from the current
wording rather than from scratch. Use Save skill to apply a change or
Use default to go back to the built-in wording. This is where to put a tone
of voice, a glossary of terms or label naming conventions. WikiHub always adds the fixed
parts itself - the answer format, the target language, the safety rules and, for pages,
the format the editor understands - so editing a skill cannot break a feature. The
built-in summary wording is written for someone who has never seen the page (its style
is adapted from the open-source tldr-skill, Apache-2.0). A new instruction applies to the
next answer; answers saved under the old one are not reused.
The model runs on the service you connect, so WikiHub only sends a request when
someone clicks.

title: Administrator Mail & Requests
text:
<>
Someone who has no account yet, or has forgotten their password, cannot sign in to
ask for help. The Contact an administrator link on the sign-in page
gives them a short form (fields marked with a red * are required: name and email; the
message is optional). WikiHub saves the request, tells
every System Administrator in the bell, shows it on everyone's
Requests page, and e-mails it to your administrator mailboxes.
Every System Administrator sees every request and any of them can handle it -
whoever gets there first. A mailbox is not needed to see or act on requests: it only
decides where the email goes. Once someone resolves a request it is resolved for
everyone, and the others' bell notifications about it clear. With no mailbox set
up, requests still arrive in the app, marked In app only; the sign-in
details from Create account / Reset password are then handed back
on screen to pass on yourself.
Set up a mailbox (System Administrators): open
Administration → Mailboxes and choose Add mailbox.
Administrator account: the account this mailbox belongs to - the
request emails go to its address and it signs the mail that account sends. Only
System Administrators can be linked, and each account has one mailbox. If that
account is disabled, its mailbox stops receiving requests automatically. (Every
System Administrator sees the requests in the app either way.)
Mailbox address, Sender name and
Provider: the sender name is optional and is the name shown as the
sender of the request emails in your mail client (leave it blank to show the
address). Pick Gmail or Outlook to fill in the server, or choose Other and
enter the
SMTP server, Port and Security
(STARTTLS is usually port 587, SSL/TLS port 465) yourself. Each mailbox has its own
settings.
Username and Password: leave the username blank to
use the address. The password is stored encrypted and is never shown again. When you
press Save, WikiHub first signs in to the mail server with these
settings, and only saves if that works. If it does not, nothing is saved and the
dialog explains what went wrong in plain words (with the server's own reply under
Technical details), so you can correct the details and try again. Gmail
needs an app password rather than your normal Google password.
Each mailbox e-mails a request to itself, so with three mailboxes an incoming request
produces three e-mails. The requester is only told about a delivery problem when
none of them could be reached.
Only a mailbox's own account, or the built-in super administrator, can edit its
settings, test it, change its password or remove it - another System Administrator
seeing it in this list has those buttons greyed out, so a mistake (or a deliberate one)
on someone else's mailbox is not possible.
Status on the Mailboxes page:
Working: the last sign-in or send succeeded.
Needs new password: the mail server rejected the password, usually
because it expired.
Can't connect / Server error: the server was
unreachable or refused the message. Not a password problem.
Switched off / Account disabled: not receiving
requests. Use the power button to switch a mailbox on or off.
When a mailbox password expires. Many mail providers require a new
password every few months. WikiHub signs in to every active mailbox once an hour. When
the server rejects a password, the mailbox's owner sees a red banner across the
top of every page with an Update password button (also available as
the key icon on the Mailboxes page). The new password is tested with the mail server
before it is saved. Other administrators do not see the banner - it is the owner's
to fix.
The mailbox pool. Every working mailbox on this page - marked
In pool next to its status - also stands in for administrators who have
none of their own. The automatic e-mails this page describes, and the ones in
Users and a space's Access tab, still go out even when the
administrator making the change has never set up a mailbox (or theirs is not connected
right now): WikiHub relays the message through one mailbox from the pool instead, chosen
automatically. The message is still signed with the acting administrator's own
name, and a reply reaches them, not whoever's mailbox happened to relay it. Nothing
goes out at all only when the pool is empty, too - no mailbox in the workspace is
currently connected.
Requests page and notification bell. An account linked to an active
mailbox gets a Requests entry under Home and Spaces in the sidebar, with a
count of unread requests. Each new request also arrives in the bell in the top
bar, like any other notification (see Notifications).
Filter by All, Unread, Open or
Resolved; each tab shows how many requests it holds. The
Request type list narrows everything to account requests, password
resets or other requests, and the tab numbers follow it. Use Rows and
the arrows under the table to page through. Opening a request with
View details marks
it read; Mark as unread undoes that, and
Mark all as read clears the lot. Read state is your own.
Mark resolved closes a request for everyone who received it, so two
administrators do not answer the same person. Reopen undoes it.
Each request shows whether the e-mail to your mailbox was sent. A request is
always saved on the Requests page, even when the e-mail could not be delivered.
Handle a request. For an account or password-reset request, the
details window has a Handle this request box with two ways to do it:
Automatically. Create account automatically creates the
account from the request (a Member, with a username taken from the e-mail address, and
a generated password) and e-mails the username and password to the requester from your
mailbox. Reset password automatically sets a generated password on the
account the request names and e-mails it. You are asked to confirm first, and the
request is marked resolved afterwards. Either way, the result sits behind a
Show details toggle with a Copy button for the
username and address - and, if the e-mail could not be sent, the password too, shown
only that once and never stored - so you can pass any of them on another way.
Manually. Create account manually opens the usual Create user
form with the requester's details already filled in; Set password manually
lets you choose (or generate) the new password yourself. WikiHub does not e-mail
anything in this case, and the request is marked resolved once you save.
The automatic reset is only offered when the e-mail in the request is the one already on
the account, so a password is never sent to an address someone merely typed. If the
address differs, the account is disabled, or it is an administrator you cannot manage,
the box says why and only the manual route is left. Nothing is offered for a request
that is already resolved, so it cannot be done twice. Both actions need the
Manage users permission and appear in the Users audit trail.
Anyone can type any e-mail address into the form. Treat it as a way to reply, not as
proof of who they are - confirm identity before creating an account or resetting a
password for someone. Emailed passwords are temporary: ask people to change them after
signing in.
What the e-mails look like. The notification your mailbox sends
itself, and the messages that give someone their new account or password, are styled
in the workspace's colours and name, with a plain-text version for clients that
cannot show it, and end with a signature (for account and password e-mails, your
own name and address). Set WIKIHUB_PUBLIC_URL (for example
https://wiki.example.com) so they can include an
Open Requests or Sign in button; left blank, those buttons are
simply left out.
Mailbox passwords are encrypted with WIKIHUB_MAIL_ENCRYPTION_KEY, or,
when that is blank, with a key derived from WIKIHUB_SECRET_KEY. If that
value changes, the stored passwords cannot be read: the mailboxes then show
Needs new password and each owner enters theirs again. The backend
and the worker must use the same value.
),

title: Safe Operation & System Troubleshooting
text:
<>
Best practices for maintaining workspace stability and resolving technical issues:
Access & Permission Issues: If a user cannot see a page
or space, check Space access, Page access restrictions,
and group membership - or just open Effective permissions
in the space's Access panel for that user and see the resolved answer
directly instead of cross-referencing all three by hand.
Upload Failures: Verify file size limits and allowed extensions under
Settings. Ensure MinIO/S3 object storage is healthy and responsive.
Import Worker Failures: Check background worker task logs, Redis queue
connectivity, and available disk space. Scanned archives can be resumed from the Backup panel.
API Documentation: Administrators can access interactive OpenAPI / Swagger
documentation at /docs and ReDoc at /redoc.
Three things people often go looking for don't exist in this build, so
it's worth knowing before you go hunting: there is no automatic invite
e-mail (accounts are created directly - see Managing Users & Groups;
someone who can't sign in can send a request from the sign-in page instead,
and an administrator can answer it from Requests by creating the account and
e-mailing the sign-in details, see Administrator Mail & Requests), no page-watch or @-mention alerts
(the bell tells you about changes to your own access and account - for page
activity the closest things are the Home activity feed and Recently
visited/worked on), and no in-app audit-log viewer (admin actions and impersonation are logged
server-side, but there is nowhere in the UI to browse that log yet).
